record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It relates downstream benchmark performance to estimated training compute, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting the original parameter/token/compute scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites neural scaling laws but does not test held-out cross-entropy power laws, small-run extrapolation, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its relevant results are the three performance-versus-cost relationships in Figure 2. Other benchmark scores and language-distribution estimates do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: Across existing open models (dense, up to 32B), the paper regresses averaged Japanese benchmark scores on log training compute (parameters × tokens), total or Japanese-only (Figure 2). This bears on V6 in a new setting: Japanese tasks and continual pre-training, with no controlled sweep. No pretraining-loss scaling or fitted allocation is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that continual pre-training improves target-language performance, but its gains match the extra Japanese-specific compute spent. It is therefore about as cost-efficient as training from scratch, even for cultural understanding. They also conclude that language-agnostic benchmark scores depend mainly on total training cost. Separately, they find open LLMs' pretraining data is heavily English-biased.
record.recipe_differences: The study relates downstream benchmark averages to estimated compute across existing models; it does not run controlled pretraining-loss scaling sweeps or fit the original laws over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The relationship depends on which cost is used: cultural-benchmark improvements look substantial against total training cost, but track Japanese training cost when that cost is isolated. The paper also notes variation from independently developed models and multiple evaluation datasets.
record.problems: The study uses independently developed models rather than a controlled training strategy and combines several evaluation datasets; the authors report R² values of 0.60 for Figure 2(a) and 0.57 for Figure 2(c). The analysis is limited to dense models up to 32B parameters, and generalization of Figure 2(c) to larger models is left for future work.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted. Figure 2 panels (a), (b), and (c) are each recorded as separate aggregate rows; the paper does not state numerical plotted values in the text.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining-loss curves over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-to-large extrapolation; the authors leave generalisation beyond 32B to future work.
No other modalities. Continual pre-training is examined only via downstream scores, not loss power laws.
No prediction from pretraining loss; no extrapolation beyond 32B; no MoE models; no languages other than Japanese.
No fitting-choice sensitivity or comparison of exponents.

missing.what: Per-model Japanese token estimates and continual-pretraining token counts that set the x-axis of Figure 2(c), plus the per-model scores behind the averages. Together these would let the plotted points be reconstructed partially.
Number of models in the Figure 2 regressions and the compute range spanned (orders of magnitude); not stated in the text.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: this is a cross-model observational regression in a new setting (Japanese, continual pre-training), not a different method aimed at the original question. Compute is the 6ND-style product of parameters and tokens. Japanese compute uses estimated language shares (Kendall τ about 0.6–0.8 against known distributions). The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or tests predicting much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization or fitted parameter/token allocation trends.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No test of power-law loss across modalities or training regimes.

Tests downstream benchmark scores against estimated total or Japanese training cost, not pretraining loss; the analysis is focused on Japanese benchmarks and does not test controlled extrapolation to much larger runs.
Reports regression R² values and study limitations, but does not test sensitivity to fitting choices, compare published exponents or compute-optimal splits, or show curves bending from a power law.

relationships.condition: Japanese cultural-understanding benchmarks plotted against total training compute, including continual-pretraining models
relationships.reason: Continual-pretraining models sit well above the total-compute trend (r2). Predictability holds only when compute is restricted to the target language, and fits are moderate (R² ~0.6; r1, r3).
relationships.display_finding: Continual-pretraining models performed well above the total-compute trend, while restricting compute to Japanese yielded moderate fits around R²=0.6.
